## The accounting

Ignoring spaces and punctuation:

- Your two Steamed Hams lines contain **112 letters**.
- The 16 original Disney titles contain **217 letters**.
- The fragments you have left contain **105 letters**.

**217 − 105 = 112.**

And the 112 missing letters are exactly the 112 letters of the two lines, as a multiset — capitals included. So every remaining character in a damaged title is a character the target text did **not** still need.

## The extraction rule

This rule reproduces your fragments exactly:

```text
need = letter counts of the Steamed Hams lines, case-sensitive

for each film title in release order:
    for each character in the title, left to right:
        if need[character] > 0:
            take it and decrease need[character]
        else:
            leave it in the title
```

So the titles were not anagrammed or reordered. Letters were deleted in place, preserving the surviving letters’ original order and word boundaries.

## Why the damage is so uneven

Because the letter budget was consumed chronologically, early films were mined heavily, while later films were barely touched. Once a letter’s quota was exhausted, every later occurrence of that letter had to stay.

| Film | Leftover | Letters taken |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1937 *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs* | `v w` | 24/26 |
| 1940 *Pinocchio* | — | 9/9 |
| 1940 *Fantasia* | — | 8/8 |
| 1941 *Dumbo* | — | 5/5 |
| 1942 *Bambi* | `Bab` | 2/5 |
| 1942 *Saludos Amigos* | `as As` | 9/13 |
| 1944 *The Three Caballeros* | `h h abas` | 12/18 |
| 1946 *Make Mine Music* | `ak M Msi` | 7/13 |
| 1947 *Fun and Fancy Free* | `F a Fanc F` | 8/15 |
| 1948 *Melody Time* | `Md im` | 6/10 |
| 1949 *The Adventures of Ichabod and Mr. Toad* | `h Advnts f Ichabod and M. Toad` | 8/31 |
| 1950 *Cinderella* | `Cinda` | 5/10 |
| 1951 *Alice in Wonderland* | `Alice in Wondeland` | 1/17 |
| 1953 *Peter Pan* | `ete an` | 3/8 |
| 1955 *Lady and the Tramp* | `Lad and the Tam` | 3/15 |
| 1959 *Sleeping Beauty* | `Sleeing Beaty` | 2/14 |

## Specific tells

- **`v w` from Snow White:** the target lines contain no lowercase `v` at all, so the `v` must survive. They need one capital `W` (“Well”) and one lowercase `w` (“welcome”), but *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs* has a capital `W` plus two lowercase `w`s, so one lowercase `w` is surplus. Everything else is consumed.
- **`Bab` from Bambi:** by 1942 the lowercase `a` and `b` quotas were already filled — `a` by earlier films such as *Snow White* and *Fantasia*, and `b` by *Dumbo*. The text contains no capital `B`, so the initial `B` also has to stay. Only the `m` and `i` could still be taken.
- **`as As` from Saludos Amigos:** lowercase `a` and `s` were no longer needed, and capital `A` never occurs in the target. The capital `S` could still be used, so it disappears.
- **`Alice in Wondeland`:** by 1951 almost every letter quota was exhausted; only the `r` was still needed. That single deletion is why “Wonderland” becomes “Wondeland.”
- **`Sleeing Beaty`:** only the `p` and `u` were still owed, producing “Sleeing” and “Beaty.”
- **`Lad and the Tam`:** only `y`, `r`, and `p` were taken.

## The capitals are load-bearing

The strange capitalization in the target is not stylistic. It specifies which capitals must come from the title-initial capitals: `maDe`, `deSPite`, `suPerinTendenT`, `chalmerS`, `welCoMe`, `hoPe`, `unForgeTTable`, etc. If you normalized the case, the extraction would no longer balance.

Likewise, capitals that the target never requests survive unchanged: Bambi’s `B`, Saludos Amigos’s `A`, Cinderella’s `C`, etc.

So the names were “destroyed beyond recognition” because the text was the positive print and the titles were the negative space: the message is made of the deleted letters, not the leftovers.
